name: The Harmon brothers' household
head: harmon_charles_l

arrival.note: Their father arrived in May 1830 and Andreas says 'his family following him the succeeding year'. The sons are part of that family on the ordinary reading, which puts them in Chicago in 1831; the source does not name them in that sentence.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not attested. The doctor's family that followed him in 1831 comprised a wife and up to nine children, four of whom died in infancy, and no source counts who travelled.

origin.note: Their father practised at Burlington from 1806, married there in 1808, was postmaster there from 1816 and left for the West after reverses in 1829. That is the family's home and the sons' presumed origin; it is not stated of them.

reason_for_coming.value: Following their father west after his business reverses
reason_for_coming.note: 'In 1829 the Doctor suffered some pecuniary reverses and resolved to attempt recuperation in the Great West.' The sons' own motive is not recorded.

works_at.note: A DISCREPANCY CARRIED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED, and it is already on the building record: Andreas names the concern 'Harmon's and Loomis's' while the 1833 advertisement is headed 'C. & I. HARMON' and names no Loomis. Those are compatible - and note that Loomis is the brothers' own middle name and their mother's maiden name, Welthyan Loomis - but they are not the same statement.

present_on_scene_date.note: Documented trading in November 1833; nothing follows the firm to 1835. Their father left for Texas in 1834 and they did not.

persons.name: Charles Loomis Harmon

occupation.note: The firm 'C. & I. HARMON' advertised dry goods, crockery, hardware and wet and dry groceries in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833, over copy dated the 18th.

persons.note: THE INITIALS ARE RESOLVED BY A SENTENCE IN ANOTHER CHAPTER, which is the find that makes this household possible. Andreas's life of Dr Elijah Dewey Harmon lists his five surviving children: 'Charles Loomis Harmon, Isaac Dewey Harmon, Harriet Harmon, Lucretia Harmon, and Welthyan Loomis Harmon.' C. and I. are therefore the doctor's two eldest sons, and the firm in the town's first newspaper is a family partnership. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Harmon, C. L.” (poll_1834_051, line 220). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Harmon' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Chas. L. Harmon” (f1839_v0709, printed page 40, ward 1). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Harmon' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins C. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.name: Isaac Dewey Harmon

occupation.note: The other half of C. & I. Harmon.

persons.note: A SEPARATE MAN FROM 'ISAAC HARMON, TOWN CLERK', OR PERHAPS NOT, AND THE RECORD WILL NOT DECIDE. The surname 'Harmon' is in Norris 1844 and no entry under it carries the initial 'I' of 'Isaac Dewey Harmon'. A surname-only agreement is a refusal. research_note: TWO BROTHERS IDENTIFIED BY CROSS-READING TWO CHAPTERS OF THE SAME BOOK, which is the kind of result this layer exists to produce: a newspaper masthead of initials becomes two named men with a father, a home town and a reason for being in Illinois. THE THIRD HARMON IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT. An Isaac Harmon was the town's clerk and collector in 1833-34 and is not written here, because Andreas's 1832 militia list carries two distinct Isaac Harmons and this project cannot tell which is which. That is a documented resident consciously left out of the count rather than guessed into it.

old_settler_deaths.the_header_admission:
Names, places * , dates, and ages at death
of some of Chicago's Old Settlers, prior to 1843, and other well - known citizens who arrived after 1843, together
with others prominently connected with Illinois history:
old_settler_deaths.note: LATER EVIDENCE OF A DEATH, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. Fergus's 1843 directory (1896) prints an obituary list of old settlers, and one of its entries meets somebody of this name. THE HEADER OF THE LIST IS QUOTED ABOVE, and it is the limit the whole reading turns on. It does not mean the person was in Chicago in 1835, and it does not mean they arrived before 1843 — the list's own header, quoted above, says it also names citizens who arrived later and others merely 'prominently connected with Illinois history'. A match means one thing: a name in the 1835 layer and a name in this list agree on surname and first initial, and the list gives that name a death date and an age. The date and the interval are the payload. Whatever is carried is carried as evidence of a DEATH and of an interval the birth falls in, never as an 1835 fact and never as a grade. T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply; this file changes no record. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. A death notice printed in 1896 says a person of this name died on a day; under the ratified ladder (T-0513) that is later evidence about a DEATH, and it is never an 1835 residence. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

people.birth_year_arithmetic: The page prints the death as 'April 9, 1886' and the age as 'aged 72'. An age of 72 completed years means at least 72 and less than 73, so the birth falls between 1813-04-10 and 1814-04-09: the birth year is 1813 or 1814. The subtraction is this project's; the page states no year of birth.

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Harmon, Isaac D., dry goods merchant, 8 Clark street'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. The street NUMBER printed against it is a number in the 1839 grid, a numbering this town's year does not have, so the street name crosses and the number does not. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `harmon_loomis_store`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 4 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1839's evidence and moves nothing.
